cards.prompt: Select just the revenue column using loc, keeping it a DataFrame instead of a Series.
cards.why: Passing a list of column names to loc keeps the result 2D, even for a single column.
cards.whenToUse: You need a one-column DataFrame rather than a Series, e.g. before a merge.
cards.commonMistake: Using df.loc[:, 'revenue'] (no list), which returns a Series instead.

cards.prompt: Select the first 3 rows by position.
cards.why: iloc slices by integer position, regardless of what the index labels actually are.
cards.whenToUse: You want rows by their position, not by a label.
cards.commonMistake: Using loc[:3], which is label-based and includes the row labeled 3 (four rows), not three.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2   West     Bags       80      8

cards.prompt: Select rows where revenue is greater than 100.
cards.why: df['revenue'] > 100 produces a boolean Series that's used to filter rows.
cards.whenToUse: Filtering rows by a condition on one or more columns.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting the outer df[...] and treating the boolean Series itself as the filtered result.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12

cards.prompt: Use region as the DataFrame's index instead of the default integer index.
cards.why: set_index() promotes a column to the index, useful before label-based lookups.
cards.whenToUse: You'll repeatedly select rows by that column's values.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting set_index() returns a new DataFrame — it doesn't modify df in place unless inplace=True is passed.
cards.example:
#        category  revenue  units
# region
# West      Shoes      120     12
# East      Shoes       95      9

cards.prompt: After setting region as the index, select every row for 'West' using loc.
cards.why: Once region is the index, loc looks it up by label directly.
cards.whenToUse: Repeated label-based lookups are cleaner once the lookup column is the index.
cards.commonMistake: Trying df.set_index('region')['West'], which looks for a column named 'West' instead of a row label.
cards.example:
#        category  revenue  units
# region
# West      Shoes      120     12
# West       Bags       80      8
# West       Bags       45      5

cards.prompt: Get the revenue value at row 0 using a fast scalar accessor (not loc).
cards.why: at is optimized for single scalar lookups by label, faster than loc for one value.
cards.whenToUse: Reading or writing exactly one cell, not a slice or a whole column.
cards.commonMistake: Using .at with a slice or list — it only works for a single scalar, unlike loc.

cards.prompt: Filter rows where revenue is over 100, using a string expression instead of boolean indexing.
cards.why: query() lets you write the filter condition as a readable string referencing column names directly.
cards.whenToUse: Longer boolean conditions where query() reads more like plain English than chained comparisons.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting quotes around the expression, or referencing a column name that doesn't exist.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12

cards.prompt: Select rows where region is either 'West' or 'East'.
cards.why: isin() checks membership against a list, cleaner than chaining multiple == comparisons with |.
cards.whenToUse: Filtering against a set of allowed values rather than a single equality check.
cards.commonMistake: Writing df['region'] == ['West', 'East'] (an invalid comparison) instead of isin().
cards.example: # 6 rows — West and East only, North excluded

cards.prompt: Select rows where revenue is between 50 and 100, inclusive.
cards.why: between() is shorthand for two chained comparisons (>= and <=) combined with &.
cards.whenToUse: Range filters on a single numeric column.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting between() is inclusive of both endpoints by default.

cards.prompt: Select rows where region is 'West' AND revenue is over 50.
cards.why: Combining conditions with & requires wrapping each condition in parentheses because of Python's operator precedence.
cards.whenToUse: Filtering on more than one column condition at once.
cards.commonMistake: Omitting the parentheses around each condition, which raises a TypeError because & binds tighter than ==.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 2   West     Bags       80      8

cards.prompt: Return a copy of df without the units column.
cards.why: drop(columns=...) removes columns without needing axis=1.
cards.whenToUse: Discarding one or more columns you don't need downstream.
cards.commonMistake: Using axis=1 with a bare list instead of the clearer columns= keyword.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue
# 0   West    Shoes      120
# 1   East    Shoes       95

cards.prompt: Remove the rows labeled 0 and 1 from df.
cards.why: drop() defaults to axis=0 (rows), matching row labels rather than positions.
cards.whenToUse: Removing specific known rows by their index label.
cards.commonMistake: Passing positions instead of labels — drop() matches index labels, which breaks after prior filtering leaves gaps in the index.
cards.example: # rows 2 through 7 remain; 0 and 1 are gone

cards.prompt: Rename the revenue column to sales.
cards.why: rename(columns={...}) maps old names to new ones without touching the rest of the DataFrame.
cards.whenToUse: Renaming one or a few columns for clarity or to match a downstream schema.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting rename() returns a new DataFrame — the original df is unchanged unless inplace=True.
cards.example:
#   region category  sales  units
# 0   West    Shoes    120     12

cards.prompt: After filtering, reset the index to a clean 0..n range without keeping the old index as a column. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: drop=True discards the old index instead of inserting it as a new column.
cards.whenToUse: Any time you filter or sort and want a tidy sequential index afterward.
cards.commonMistake: Omitting drop=True, which leaves the old index as an 'index' column you usually don't want.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2   West     Bags       80      8
# 3   East    Shoes       70      7
# 4  North     Bags       65      6

cards.prompt: Which correctly selects rows at integer positions 1 and 2 (not by label)?
cards.why: iloc uses exclusive-end position slicing, so 1:3 selects positions 1 and 2; loc uses inclusive label slicing, so 1:3 would include the row labeled 3 too.
cards.whenToUse: Precisely picking rows by position rather than by index label.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming loc and iloc slice the same way — loc's upper bound is inclusive, iloc's is exclusive.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9
# 2   West     Bags       80      8
